why_how.text: Night driving is harder because headlights show less of the road and oncoming glare hides it, so Missouri sets clear headlight rules.
Knowing how far your lights reach and when to dim keeps your speed and beams matched to the road.

scenario.text: Carlos drives home on a dark two-lane road with high beams on, and a car appears ahead coming toward him.

reasoning.text: High beams are for when no vehicles are coming toward you; for an oncoming vehicle you dim within five hundred feet, about one block.

result.text: Carlos switches to low beams by the time the car is within five hundred feet.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking headlights are only required after dark.

correction.text: Missouri also requires headlights any time the weather calls for windshield wipers, in addition to the clock rule.

memory_support.text: Lights reach about three hundred fifty feet; dim at five hundred oncoming, three hundred following.

prompt.text: Carlos is following another car at night with his high beams on. Within what distance of that car should he dim to low beams?

answer.text: Within three hundred feet of the vehicle he is following.

rationale.text: The five hundred foot distance is for oncoming vehicles; when following, the guide says dim within three hundred feet.

lines.text: Night hides more of the road.
Headlights follow two rules.
Beams and speed must fit.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving at night and the headlight rules that go with it. Night driving is harder for two reasons the guide spells out: headlights show less of the road ahead and to the sides than daylight does, and the glare from oncoming vehicles makes the road harder to see. Because of that, Missouri ties your headlights to both the clock and the weather. We will also look at how far headlights actually let you see, when to use high beams, the two distances for dimming them, and a few night habits such as following the edgeline, slowing for curves and staying alert enough to drive.

lines.text: Headlights show less ahead and to the sides.
Oncoming glare hides the road.
Keep windows and lights clean and aimed.

narration.text: Start with why night driving takes extra care. In daylight you see the whole road and its edges. At night your headlights show less of the road ahead and to the sides, and when another vehicle comes toward you, its glare makes the road harder to see. You can help yourself before the drive even starts. The guide says to keep your windows and headlights clean, to make sure the lights work, and to have their aim checked from time to time. Clean glass and clean, working, well-aimed lights give you the most of the limited view that headlights provide, which is why this simple care belongs to night driving.

lines.text: Clock: half an hour after sunset.
Until half an hour before sunrise.
Weather: whenever wipers are needed.

narration.text: Missouri gives you two separate reasons to turn your headlights on. The first is the clock. Headlights must be on from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise. Notice that the window does not start exactly at sunset or end exactly at sunrise; it runs from half an hour past sunset to half an hour before sunrise. The second reason is the weather. Missouri requires headlights any time the weather calls for using your windshield wipers, so a rainy afternoon counts even in full daylight. Keep both triggers in mind together: one is set by the clock, and the other is set by the wipers.

lines.text: High beams when no one is coming.
Dim within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic.
Dim within three hundred feet when following.

narration.text: High beams are the tool for empty roads. The guide says use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you. Once another vehicle shows up, you dim, and there are two distances to learn. For an oncoming vehicle, dim to low beams within five hundred feet, which the guide describes as about one block. When you are following another vehicle, dim to low beams within three hundred feet. So the oncoming distance is the longer one, about a block, and the following distance is the shorter one. Picture the block-length gap for a car coming toward you and the shorter gap for the car in front of you.

lines.text: Headlights reach about three hundred fifty feet.
Stop or turn within that range.
Match speed to what you can see.

narration.text: Headlights let you see only about three hundred fifty feet ahead. At night, that is the whole of your view down the road. Overdriving your headlights means going so fast that you could not stop or turn within that range. The guide's rule is not to overdrive them: keep a speed at which you can stop or turn within about three hundred fifty feet. Combine this with the reason night driving is harder in the first place, that headlights show less of the road ahead and to the sides than daylight does. A shorter view calls for a speed that lets you stop or turn inside it, and that speed is your choice to make.

lines.text: About three hundred fifty feet: how far you see.
Five hundred feet: dim for oncoming traffic.
Three hundred feet: dim when following.

narration.text: This is the trap of the lesson. Three night distances are easy to mix up because they are close together. Headlights reach about three hundred fifty feet, and that number is about how far you can see, which sets your speed. Five hundred feet, about one block, is when you dim for oncoming traffic. Three hundred feet is when you dim while following another vehicle. A question may offer three hundred fifty as a dimming distance, or swap the oncoming and following numbers. Sort them by job: one tells you how far your lights reach, and the other two tell you when to switch down to low beams.

lines.text: Carlos follows a car at night.
His high beams are on.
When must he dim?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Carlos is driving at night with his high beams on, and he comes up behind another car traveling in the same direction. Within what distance of that car should he dim to low beams? Work it out before reading on. The answer is within three hundred feet. That is the distance for following another vehicle. The five hundred foot distance, about one block, is for a vehicle coming toward you, and about three hundred fifty feet is how far headlights let you see, not a dimming point. Once Carlos is within three hundred feet of the car ahead, low beams are the rule.

lines.text: Follow the edgeline, or center line if none.
Slow for curves at the posted maximum.
Do not drive if tired.

narration.text: To close, a few habits for the drive itself. At night, follow the edgeline, or the center line if there is no edgeline, and watch for signs and for people and vehicles stopped beside the road. If you are already driving at the posted maximum, slow down for curves at night. And stay awake and alert at night; do not drive if you feel tired. Put these together with the headlight rules: lights on from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise and whenever wipers are needed, high beams when no one is coming, and low beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and three hundred feet when following.

why_how.text: Winter driving starts before you move: working wipers and defroster, and clear windows and lights.
Snow and ice change how you start, how you free spinning tires, where helpers stand, how fast you go and how you test the road.

scenario.text: Nora's car is covered in snow, and she has only a short drive to the store.

reasoning.text: The guide says never set off, however short the trip, until the windows are clear, and to clear snow and ice from windows, headlights and taillights.

result.text: Nora clears every window plus the headlights and taillights before she leaves.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking snow-rated tires or chains make normal speeds safe on snow or ice.

correction.text: Tires and chains help, but no vehicle can be driven safely on snow or ice at normal speeds, so slow down and skip cruise control.

memory_support.text: Clear the glass, start smooth, rock free, test brake.

prompt.text: Nora's tires spin as she tries to leave her snowy driveway, and her neighbor offers to stand behind the car and watch the wheels. What should she do?

answer.text: Keep the neighbor out of line with the wheels, rock gently back and forth to clear a path, and spread salt, sand or cat litter if needed.

rationale.text: Spinning wheels can throw gravel or ice and hurt someone, so nobody should stand in line with them.

lines.text: Prepare the car first.
Start out gently.
Test the road once moving.

narration.text: This lesson is about getting ready for winter roads and getting under way safely. Before winter driving, make sure the windshield wipers and defroster both work, and before any trip, clear the snow and ice from your windows, headlights and taillights. Then we will look at tires and chains, why speed still has to come down on snow and ice, how to start out slowly and smoothly, what to do when the tires spin, why nobody should stand in line with spinning wheels, and how a gentle touch of the brakes tells you how slippery the road is once you are moving.

lines.text: Check wipers and defroster before winter.
Clear windows, headlights and taillights.
Never leave until windows are clear.

narration.text: Preparation comes first. Before winter driving, make sure the windshield wipers and the defroster both work. Then, each time it snows, clear all snow and ice from the windows, the headlights and the taillights. The lights are on the list, not only the glass. The guide is firm about leaving early: never set off, however short the trip, until the windows are clear. A quick drive to a nearby store is still a trip, so the rule still applies. Clear windows all around, clear headlights and taillights, working wipers and a working defroster are the starting point for every winter drive.

lines.text: Snow-rated tires or chains help.
No vehicle is safe at normal speeds on snow or ice.
Slow down and skip cruise control.

narration.text: Next, equipment and speed. Snow-rated tires or chains help on winter roads. If your vehicle lacks snow-rated tires, keep chains ready to put on in bad weather. But equipment has a limit. The guide says no vehicle can be driven safely on snow or ice at normal speeds, so slow down, and do not use cruise control. That holds whether you have snow-rated tires, chains or neither. Tires and chains are a help, not permission to drive at your usual speed. So the plan has two parts: the right tires or chains ready to go, and a slower speed without cruise control once the road is covered in snow or ice.

lines.text: Accelerate slowly and smoothly.
If tires spin, rock gently back and forth.
Spread salt, sand or cat litter if needed.

narration.text: Now starting out. When starting out on snow or ice, accelerate slowly and smoothly. Sometimes the tires spin anyway. If your tires spin when starting on snow, rock gently back and forth to clear a path. If that is not enough, spread salt, sand or cat litter around the wheels. Notice the word gently: the guide is describing a gentle rocking motion to clear a path, not more power. The same smooth touch that gets you started comes back once you are moving, when you test the road with the brakes. Slow, smooth acceleration first, gentle rocking if needed, and then salt, sand or cat litter under the wheels as a backup.

lines.text: Spinning wheels throw gravel or ice.
Never let anyone stand in line with them.
Rock gently to clear a path.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a car is stuck and the tires are spinning, a helper may want to stand right behind or beside the wheels to watch or push. The guide says never let anyone stand in line with spinning wheels, because they can throw gravel or ice and hurt someone. The spinning tire itself is the hazard to a person standing in its line. So if you are stuck, keep everyone out of line with the wheels, rock gently back and forth to clear a path, and spread salt, sand or cat litter around the wheels if needed. Freeing the car never calls for putting a person in line with a spinning wheel.

lines.text: Nora's tires spin on snow.
A neighbor offers to stand behind.
What should she do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Nora is trying to leave her snowy driveway, and her tires spin. Her neighbor offers to stand right behind the car to watch the wheels while she tries again. What should Nora do? Work it out before reading on. She should keep her neighbor out of line with the wheels, because spinning wheels can throw gravel or ice and hurt someone. Then she should rock gently back and forth to clear a path, and if the car still will not move, spread salt, sand or cat litter around the wheels. Once she is moving, she can brake gently to test how slippery the road is and set her speed to match.

lines.text: Brake gently once moving.
Judge how slippery it is.
Set your speed to match.

narration.text: To close, the first thing to do once you are rolling. Once moving on snow or ice, brake gently to test how slippery the road is, and set your speed to match. That small test tells you what the road will allow. Then recall the whole winter routine from this lesson: wipers and defroster working before the season, snow and ice cleared from windows, headlights and taillights before every trip, snow-rated tires or chains ready, slower speeds with no cruise control, slow and smooth acceleration, gentle rocking if the tires spin, and nobody in line with spinning wheels. Next we look at stopping on snow and ice.

why_how.text: Stopping takes longer on snow or ice, so the gap ahead grows and braking must be gentle.
Ice hides in predictable places, and four-wheel drive does not make ice safe.

scenario.text: Ray drives a four-wheel drive truck across an overpass on a cold morning after the road was cleared.

reasoning.text: Overpasses freeze before the rest of the road, ice patches may remain on cleared roads, and four-wheel drive should not be used on ice.

result.text: Ray expects ice on the overpass, and if he hits ice in four-wheel drive he lifts his foot off the accelerator.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking hard on a slippery road to stop sooner.

correction.text: Brake gently and smoothly; slamming the brakes can cause a skid, and on very slick surfaces you pump unless your manual gives anti-lock instructions.

memory_support.text: Long gap, soft brakes, bridges freeze first.

prompt.text: Ray is following a car on a snowy road. About how much time should he leave between them, and why?

answer.text: About eight to ten seconds, because stopping takes longer on snow or ice.

rationale.text: The longer stopping on snow or ice is the reason the safe gap grows to about eight to ten seconds.

lines.text: Stopping takes longer on snow and ice.
Brake gently and smoothly.
Expect ice on bridges.

narration.text: This lesson is about stopping and handling ice once you are on a winter road. On snow or ice, stopping takes longer, and that one fact shapes most of what follows. It is why the guide asks for a much longer gap to the vehicle ahead, and why it asks for gentle, smooth braking rather than slamming the brakes. We will also cover where ice tends to wait for you, starting with bridges and overpasses, which freeze before the rest of the road, and patches that remain even on cleared roads. Finally, we will see why four-wheel drive is not the answer on ice, and what to do if you hit ice in four-wheel drive.

lines.text: Stopping takes longer on snow or ice.
Leave about eight to ten seconds ahead.
The gap grows because stops grow.

narration.text: Start with following distance. On snow or ice, stopping takes longer, so leave about eight to ten seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. The reason and the rule go together: the safe gap to the vehicle ahead grows to about eight to ten seconds because stopping takes longer. The guide gives this gap as time, in seconds, rather than as a distance. When the road is covered in snow or ice, treat that eight to ten second cushion as your normal setting, because a longer stop needs more room in front of you. Put simply, longer stops on snow and ice call for a longer gap, and the guide sets that gap at about eight to ten seconds.

lines.text: Brake gently and smoothly on slippery roads.
Slamming the brakes can cause a skid.
Bridges and overpasses freeze first.

narration.text: Braking on slippery roads should be gentle and smooth. Slamming the brakes can cause a skid. On very slick surfaces, the guide says you pump the brakes, unless your manual gives anti-lock instructions, so check the manual if your vehicle has anti-lock brakes. Next, know where ice waits. Bridges and overpasses freeze before the rest of the road, so an overpass can be icy before the road around it freezes. And patches of ice may remain even on cleared roads, so a plowed road is not a promise of an ice-free one. Gentle braking and an eye on bridges, overpasses and leftover patches go together on winter roads.

lines.text: Do not use four-wheel drive on ice.
Such vehicles can easily roll over there.
Hit ice in it? Lift off the accelerator.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers assume four-wheel drive makes ice safe. The guide says the opposite: do not use four-wheel drive on ice, where such vehicles can easily roll over. If you do hit ice while in four-wheel drive, lift your foot off the accelerator. Notice that the response is to lift off, not to press harder or to brake hard, which on a slippery road can cause a skid. So four-wheel drive belongs off the ice, and the moment you find yourself on ice in four-wheel drive, your foot comes off the accelerator. Combine that with the warning about bridges and overpasses, which freeze before the rest of the road.

lines.text: Ray follows a car on snow.
How much time should he leave?
What is the reason?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ray is following another car on a snowy road. About how much time should he leave between his car and the car ahead, and what is the reason the guide gives? Work it out before reading on. The answer is about eight to ten seconds. The reason is that stopping takes longer on snow or ice, so the safe gap to the vehicle ahead grows to about eight to ten seconds. If Ray also needs to slow down, he should brake gently and smoothly, because slamming the brakes can cause a skid, and he should watch for bridges and overpasses, which freeze before the rest of the road.

lines.text: About eight to ten seconds of gap.
Gentle brakes; pump on very slick surfaces.
Bridges freeze first; no four-wheel drive on ice.

narration.text: To close, here is winter stopping in one picture. Leave about eight to ten seconds between you and the vehicle ahead, because stopping takes longer on snow or ice. Brake gently and smoothly, since slamming the brakes can cause a skid, and on very slick surfaces pump the brakes unless your manual gives anti-lock instructions. Expect bridges and overpasses to freeze before the rest of the road, and expect patches of ice even on cleared roads. Do not use four-wheel drive on ice, where such vehicles can easily roll over, and if you hit ice in four-wheel drive, lift your foot off the accelerator. Next we move from ice to rain.

why_how.text: Rain makes a slick film and longer stops, and tires can end up riding on water instead of the road.
Knowing how to respond and how to prevent hydroplaning keeps the tires on the road.

scenario.text: Tom is on the highway in a heavy rain and thinks his tires are riding on water.

reasoning.text: That is hydroplaning, tires riding on water instead of the road; the guide says ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking.

result.text: Tom eases off the accelerator and lets the car slow without touching the brake.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking firmly the moment you think the car is hydroplaning.

correction.text: Ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking, because braking while hydroplaning could cause a skid.

memory_support.text: Above thirty-five it can start; at fifty-five in a storm, contact can go.

prompt.text: Tom is driving in heavy rain and thinks his tires are riding on water. What should he do with the accelerator and the brake?

answer.text: Ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking.

rationale.text: Braking while hydroplaning could cause a skid, so the guide says slow down by easing off the accelerator.

lines.text: First rain makes a slick film.
Tires can ride on water.
Respond, then prevent.

narration.text: This lesson covers wet pavement and hydroplaning. Rain changes the road surface in ways that are easy to underestimate. When rain starts, water mixes with road dust and oil into a slick film, wet leaves turn slippery, and stopping takes longer. Wet pavement also makes it harder to stay on the road through curves. Then there is hydroplaning, when tires ride on water instead of the road. We will cover the two speeds the guide names for it, what to do if you think you are hydroplaning, and how good tires, slower speeds and leaving cruise control off help prevent it in the first place.

lines.text: Water, dust and oil form a slick film.
Wet leaves turn slippery.
Slow down and add following distance.

narration.text: Start with the moment the rain begins. When rain starts, water mixes with road dust and oil into a slick film. Wet leaves turn slippery too. And stopping takes longer on wet pavement. The guide's response to all of that is to slow down and add following distance. Curves need attention as well, because wet pavement also makes it harder to stay on the road through curves. So the start of a rain shower is not a time to relax. The road surface has just become slicker, your stops have become longer, and curves have become harder to hold, so your speed comes down and the gap ahead grows.

lines.text: Cruise control keeps powering the wheels.
It keeps going after traction is lost.
That can make you lose control.

narration.text: Cruise control is a habit worth breaking in the rain. Do not use cruise control on wet pavement, because it keeps powering the wheels after traction is lost, and that can make you lose control. In other words, cruise control goes on pushing the wheels even once the tires have stopped gripping. That is why no cruise control shows up again in the list of ways to prevent hydroplaning, beside good tires and slower speeds in rain. On winter roads the guide gave the same advice for snow and ice. Wet or frozen, a slippery road is a road where you keep your own foot in charge of the power instead of the cruise control.

lines.text: Tires ride on water instead of the road.
Possible at any speed over thirty-five miles per hour.
Heavy storm: all contact can go at fifty-five.

narration.text: Hydroplaning is when tires ride on water instead of the road. The guide gives two speeds to remember. It can happen at any speed over thirty-five miles per hour, which is the onset, the point above which it can begin. And in a heavy storm, tires can lose all contact with the road at fifty-five miles per hour, which is the full loss of contact. Keep these apart. Thirty-five is where hydroplaning can begin. Fifty-five is where, in a severe storm, the tires may lose contact with the road entirely. Slower speeds in rain are part of preventing it, alongside good, deep-tread tires at proper pressure.

lines.text: Ease off the accelerator.
Slow down without braking.
Braking could cause a skid.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a car starts to hydroplane, the instinct is to hit the brake. The guide says if you think you are hydroplaning, ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking, because braking could cause a skid. So the pedal you use is the accelerator, and the action is to ease off it. The car slows because you have stopped feeding it power, not because you braked. This is close to the advice for a skid, where you lift off the accelerator and do not hit the brakes. Questions may offer firm braking, holding speed with cruise control, or speeding up; each of those goes against the guide.

lines.text: Tom is in heavy rain.
He thinks his tires ride on water.
What does he do with the pedals?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Tom is driving in heavy rain on the highway, and he thinks his tires have started riding on water instead of the road. What should he do with the accelerator, and what should he do about the brake? Work it out before reading on. Tom should ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking. Braking while hydroplaning could cause a skid. He also should not have cruise control on in the first place, because on wet pavement it keeps powering the wheels after traction is lost. Hydroplaning can happen at any speed over thirty-five miles per hour, so slower speeds in rain help too.

lines.text: Good, deep-tread tires.
Proper tire pressure.
Slower speeds in rain, no cruise control.

narration.text: To close, prevention. You can prevent hydroplaning with good, deep-tread tires at proper pressure, slower speeds in rain, and no cruise control. Each of those links back to this lesson. Slower speeds matter because hydroplaning can happen at any speed over thirty-five miles per hour, and in a heavy storm tires can lose all contact at fifty-five. No cruise control matters because it keeps powering the wheels after traction is lost. And remember the rest of wet-road driving: the first rain makes a slick film of water, dust and oil, wet leaves turn slippery, stopping takes longer, and curves become harder, so slow down and add following distance.

why_how.text: Anti-lock brakes need steady pressure, which differs from the winter advice to pump on very slick surfaces.
A skid is handled the same way in any drive type, by lifting off the gas and steering where the rear slides.

scenario.text: Ines brakes hard in her anti-lock car to avoid a stopped car, and the pedal pulses and makes noise.

reasoning.text: Anti-lock brakes keep the wheels from locking, and the guide says keep firm, steady pressure while steering, do not pump, and do not be alarmed by noise or slight pulsing.

result.text: Ines keeps firm, steady pressure and steers around the stopped car.

claim.text: Common mistake: pumping anti-lock brakes in a hard stop.

correction.text: With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal while you steer; do not pump the brakes.

memory_support.text: Anti-lock: press and steer. Skid: steer the way the rear slides.

prompt.text: The rear of Ines's front-wheel drive car slides left on a wet road. What should she do with the accelerator, the brake and the wheel?

answer.text: Lift off the accelerator, do not hit the brakes, and gently steer left, the direction the rear wheels are sliding.

rationale.text: Skids are handled the same in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles, and braking hard or jerking the wheel only makes it worse.

lines.text: Anti-lock brakes stop wheel lock.
Steady pressure, no pumping.
Skids: lift off, steer gently.

narration.text: This lesson covers anti-lock brakes and skids. Four-wheel anti-lock brakes keep the wheels from locking in emergency braking, and using them well means keeping firm, steady pressure on the pedal instead of pumping. That can seem to clash with the winter advice to pump the brakes on very slick surfaces, so we will sort out how the guide handles both. Then we turn to skids. A skid is handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles: lift off the accelerator and do not hit the brakes, then gently steer in the direction the rear wheels are sliding. We will finish with the guide's four-step skid diagram.

lines.text: Wheels do not lock in emergency braking.
The pedal may pulse under hard braking.
Mechanical noise is no cause for alarm.

narration.text: Four-wheel anti-lock brakes keep the wheels from locking in emergency braking. When you brake hard, you may feel the pedal pulse under your foot. The guide says to keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal while you steer, not to pump the brakes, and not to be alarmed by mechanical noise or slight pulsing. So a hard stop in a car with anti-lock brakes has a simple shape: press firmly, keep that pressure steady, and steer where you need to go. Lifting off because the pedal pulses, or pumping it on and off, works against what the guide describes. Firm, steady pressure while you steer is the anti-lock rule.

lines.text: Very slick surfaces: the winter page says pump.
Anti-lock vehicle: check the owner's manual.
Working anti-lock brakes: firm, steady pressure.

narration.text: Here is where two pieces of advice meet. On slippery roads the guide says brake gently and smoothly, and on very slick surfaces you pump the brakes, unless your manual gives anti-lock instructions. On very slippery surfaces the winter page says to pump, but for a vehicle with anti-lock brakes it points you to the owner's manual for special situations. The anti-lock section itself is clear about a hard stop: keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal while you steer, and do not pump. So pumping belongs to the general winter advice, and an anti-lock vehicle follows its manual and the steady-pressure rule. Read which kind of brakes a question describes.

lines.text: Front-wheel or rear-wheel drive: same steps.
Lift off the accelerator.
Do not hit the brakes.

narration.text: Now skids. The guide says a skid is handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles, so you do not need to work out which wheels drive your car before you react. In both, the first steps are to lift off the accelerator and not to hit the brakes. That matches advice elsewhere in this chapter. When hydroplaning, you ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking, because braking could cause a skid, and on slippery roads slamming the brakes can cause a skid too. So in a skid, the power comes off and the brakes are left alone. The next step, steering, is where the direction of the slide matters.

lines.text: Gently steer the way the rear wheels slide.
Do not brake hard or jerk the wheel.
Those only make it worse.

narration.text: In a skid, gently steer in the direction the rear wheels are sliding. If the rear of the car slides to the right, you steer gently to the right. Do it without braking hard or jerking the wheel, which only makes the skid worse. The guide's skid diagram shows the same idea in four captioned steps: before the skid, rear wheels sliding right, front wheels turned right, and then the vehicle straight again. Read the caption as a short story. The rear slides right, the driver turns the front wheels right, toward the slide, and the car comes back to straight. Gentle steering, no hard braking, and no jerking of the wheel.

lines.text: Ines drives front-wheel drive on a wet road.
The rear slides left.
Accelerator, brake, wheel: what now?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ines drives a front-wheel drive car, and on a wet road the rear of the car begins to slide to the left. What should she do with the accelerator, the brake and the steering wheel? Work it out before reading on. She should lift off the accelerator and not hit the brakes, then gently steer to the left, the direction the rear wheels are sliding. The front-wheel drive does not change anything, because the guide says a skid is handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles. And she should not brake hard or jerk the wheel, which only makes the skid worse.

lines.text: Anti-lock: firm, steady pressure while steering.
Very slick surfaces: pump unless your manual says otherwise.
Skid: lift off, no brakes, steer toward the slide.

narration.text: To close, here is the lesson in brief. Four-wheel anti-lock brakes keep the wheels from locking in emergency braking, and you may feel the pedal pulse. With them, keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal while you steer, do not pump, and do not be alarmed by noise or slight pulsing. The winter advice to pump applies on very slick surfaces, with anti-lock vehicles pointed to the owner's manual. In a skid, in front-wheel or rear-wheel drive alike, lift off the accelerator, do not hit the brakes, and gently steer in the direction the rear wheels are sliding until the vehicle is straight again. Next we cover fog and emergencies.

why_how.text: Fog cuts how well you can see, so speed and beam choice change, and very thick fog means pulling off.
In any emergency the first rule is not to panic, and brake failure has its own pumping sequence.

scenario.text: Hal presses the brake on a downhill road and the pedal sinks to the floor.

reasoning.text: The guide says pump the pedal fast and hard several times, then apply the parking brake gradually and shift to a low gear while looking for a place to stop.

result.text: Hal pumps, eases on the parking brake, shifts down, stops off the road and calls for help instead of driving to a garage.

claim.text: Common mistake: switching to high beams in fog to see farther.

correction.text: In fog, use low beams, because high beams make it harder to see; slow down and be ready to stop.

memory_support.text: Fog: low and slow. Failed brakes: pump, parking brake, low gear.

prompt.text: Hal's brake pedal sinks to the floor. In what order does the guide list his next steps?

answer.text: Pump the pedal fast and hard several times, then apply the parking brake gradually and shift to a low gear while looking for a place to stop.

rationale.text: Brake failure is the one emergency where you pump fast and hard, the opposite of steady anti-lock pressure.

lines.text: Fog: slow down, low beams.
Emergencies: do not panic.
Brake failure: pump fast and hard.

narration.text: This lesson covers fog and the first of the vehicle emergencies. In fog, you slow down, stay ready to stop and use low beams, and if the fog gets so thick that you cannot see, you pull off the road. Then we move to emergencies. The most important rule in any emergency is not to panic, and staying calm helps you remember what to do. One emergency stands apart in how you use the brake pedal: brake failure, where you pump the pedal fast and hard. We will go through that sequence step by step, and then what to do with the vehicle once it has stopped.

lines.text: Slow down and be ready to stop.
Use low beams in fog.
High beams make it harder to see.

narration.text: In fog, slow down and be ready to stop. Use low beams, because high beams make it harder to see. This is one of the places where the high beam habit from night driving must be switched off. At night on an empty road you use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you, but fog changes that: low beams are the rule. If the fog gets so thick that you cannot see, pull off the road, stop, and leave your lights and emergency flashers on. So fog has two levels. In ordinary fog you slow down with low beams. In fog too thick to see through, you leave the road, stop, and keep your lights and flashers on.

lines.text: Not panicking is the most important rule.
Calm helps you remember what to do.
Ignition stays on until fully stopped.

narration.text: Every emergency in this chapter starts with the same rule. The most important rule in any emergency is not to panic. Staying calm in an emergency helps you remember what to do, and the rest of this lesson and the next one are full of steps worth remembering. The same fact carries a warning about the ignition. With power steering or a locking steering wheel, never turn off the ignition until you are fully stopped. That warning comes back later with the stuck accelerator, where turning off the key locks the steering in many vehicles. Calm first, then the steps, and the key stays on while the car is still moving.

lines.text: Pump the pedal fast and hard several times.
Apply the parking brake gradually.
Shift to a low gear; look for a stop.

narration.text: If the brake pedal sinks to the floor, the guide gives a clear sequence. First, pump the pedal fast and hard several times. Then apply the parking brake gradually, not all at once. Shift to a low gear, and look for a place to stop while you do. After a brake failure, get the vehicle off the road and call for help, instead of driving to a garage. That last step matters because once the car has stopped, a driver may be tempted to limp on to a repair shop. The guide says to call for help instead. Pump, apply the parking brake gradually, shift to a low gear, find a place to stop, and then call for help.

lines.text: Brake failure: pump fast and hard.
Working anti-lock brakes: firm, steady pressure.
Opposite actions on the same pedal.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Brake failure is the one emergency here where you pump the pedal fast and hard, which is the opposite of the steady pressure used with working anti-lock brakes. With anti-lock brakes that work, you keep firm, steady pressure while you steer and do not pump. When the pedal sinks to the floor, you pump it fast and hard several times. Questions like to swap these. If a question says the brakes are working and the car has anti-lock brakes, the answer is steady pressure. If it says the pedal has sunk to the floor, the answer starts with pumping, then the parking brake gradually and a low gear.

lines.text: Hal's brake pedal sinks to the floor.
What are his steps, in order?
What happens after he stops?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Hal presses his brake pedal and it sinks all the way to the floor. In what order does the guide list his next steps, and what should he do once the car has stopped? Work it out before reading on. First he pumps the pedal fast and hard several times. Then he applies the parking brake gradually and shifts to a low gear while looking for a place to stop. Once stopped, he gets the vehicle off the road and calls for help instead of driving to a garage. This is the one emergency where pumping fast and hard is right, the opposite of steady anti-lock pressure.

lines.text: Fog: slow, ready to stop, low beams.
Too thick to see: pull off, lights on.
No brakes: pump, parking brake, low gear.

narration.text: To close, here is what to carry forward. In fog, slow down, be ready to stop, and use low beams, because high beams make it harder to see. If the fog gets so thick that you cannot see, pull off the road, stop, and leave your lights and emergency flashers on. In any emergency, do not panic, because staying calm helps you remember what to do, and with power steering or a locking wheel never turn off the ignition until fully stopped. If the brake pedal sinks, pump it fast and hard, apply the parking brake gradually, shift to a low gear, stop off the road and call for help. Next come blowouts and other failures.

why_how.text: Blowouts and steering failures share a rule: hold on, lift off and wait to brake.
Running off the edge, failed headlights and a raised hood each have a short step list.

scenario.text: Sara hears a loud bang, then repeated thumping, and her steering wheel jerks on the highway.

reasoning.text: Those are signs of a blowout, so the guide says grip the wheel firmly and lift off the accelerator without braking.

result.text: Sara lets the car slow until it is nearly stopped and off the road before braking, then turns on her flashers.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking hard right after a blowout.

correction.text: Lift off the accelerator without braking, and brake only once the car is nearly stopped and off the road.

memory_support.text: Blowout or no steering: hold, coast, brake late.

prompt.text: Sara's right wheels drop off the paved edge at highway speed. What should she do before steering back?

answer.text: Hold the wheel tightly, ease off the gas without braking hard, and wait until she has slowed, has control and the lane is clear.

rationale.text: The wheels may pull to the right, so a firm grip and only gentle braking if needed come before steering back.

lines.text: Blowouts and steering failures.
Wheels off the paved edge.
Failed headlights, hood or wipers.

narration.text: This lesson covers sudden failures while you drive. We begin with a tire blowout, how it may announce itself and how to handle it without early braking. Then we look at what to do after a blowout, once the car is stopped. Next comes running off the paved edge, when your wheels drop onto the shoulder, and then a steering failure, which shares a braking rule with the blowout: in both, you wait to brake until you are nearly stopped. We finish with failed headlights, and with a hood that flies up or wipers that fail. In each case the guide gives a short list of steps, and most of them end with the flashers on and the car off the road.

lines.text: Signs: a bang, thumping, a jerking wheel.
Grip the wheel firmly.
Lift off the gas without braking.

narration.text: A blowout may announce itself with a loud bang followed by a repeated thumping, and the steering wheel may jerk. When that happens, grip the wheel firmly and lift off the accelerator without braking. Let the car slow until it is nearly stopped and off the road, and only then brake. The order matters. Gripping the wheel comes first, since the steering wheel may jerk. Lifting off the accelerator lets the car slow by itself. Braking waits until the car is nearly stopped and off the road. Grip the wheel, lift off, let it slow, and brake late: that is the blowout sequence the guide gives you.

lines.text: Hold the wheel tightly.
Ease off the gas; do not brake hard.
Steer back once slowed and clear.

narration.text: If your wheels drop off the paved edge, hold the wheel tightly and ease off the gas without braking hard. When wheels run off the paved edge, they may pull to the right, which is why the grip matters, and you use only gentle braking if any is needed. Then steer back once you have slowed, you have control, and the lane is clear. Notice that steering back is the last step, not the first. Firm grip, ease off the gas, gentle braking only if it is needed, and a return to the lane once you have slowed, you are in control and the lane is clear. That is the full sequence for running off the pavement.

lines.text: Lift off the accelerator.
Let it slow on its own.
No braking until nearly stopped, unless you must.

narration.text: If the steering fails, lift off the accelerator. Let the vehicle slow on its own, without braking until it is nearly stopped, unless you must brake sooner. And turn on the flashers. This looks a lot like the blowout response. In both, your foot comes off the accelerator first, and the car is allowed to slow by itself before the brakes come in. The difference is the small exception for steering failure, unless you must, which the blowout steps do not include. So for a steering failure: lift off, let the vehicle slow, hold the brakes until nearly stopped unless you must, and switch on the flashers.

lines.text: Blowout: brake only when nearly stopped.
Steering failure: same wait, unless you must.
Neither starts with hard braking.

narration.text: Here is the trap. After a blowout you brake only when nearly stopped, and after a steering failure you also wait to brake until nearly stopped unless you must. Questions often offer hard braking as the first step for one of them. It is wrong for both. The shared pattern is to lift off the accelerator and let the vehicle slow on its own. The difference is small: the steering failure rule allows braking sooner if you must, while the blowout rule says let the car slow until it is nearly stopped and off the road before braking. Keep these two together, and keep them apart from brake failure, where you pump the pedal fast and hard.

lines.text: Headlights fail: try the dimmer or headlight switch.
Then parking lights, flashers or turn signals.
Hood up or wipers out: window down, pull off.

narration.text: Two more failures. If the headlights fail, first try the dimmer or headlight switch. If that does not bring them back, switch on parking lights, flashers or turn signals, and pull off the road with the flashers left on. If the hood flies up or the wipers fail, your view ahead is blocked. Roll down the window to see around the blockage, turn on the flashers, and pull off the road. Both of these share an ending with most of this lesson: flashers on and the vehicle off the road. The difference is the first step, the switches for failed headlights and the open window for a raised hood or failed wipers.

lines.text: Sara's right wheels drop off the edge.
She is at highway speed.
What comes before steering back?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Sara is driving at highway speed when her right wheels drop off the paved edge onto the shoulder. What should she do before she steers back onto the road? Work it out before reading on. She should hold the wheel tightly, because the wheels may pull to the right, and ease off the gas without braking hard, using only gentle braking if any is needed. She steers back only once she has slowed, has control and the lane is clear. Jerking the wheel back at once, braking hard, or speeding up to climb back on would all go against the steps the guide gives for running off the pavement.

lines.text: Turn on the emergency flashers.
Change the tire only if it is safe.
Pull off the road first.

narration.text: To close, the moment after a blowout. Once the car is stopped off the road, turn on the emergency flashers and change the tire only if you can do it without putting yourself in danger. Then gather the lesson. A blowout may come with a bang, thumping and a jerking wheel: grip the wheel, lift off without braking, and brake only when nearly stopped and off the road. A steering failure also waits to brake until nearly stopped, unless you must. Off the paved edge, hold tight and ease off before steering back. Failed headlights, a raised hood or failed wipers end with flashers on and the car pulled off the road.

why_how.text: A stuck accelerator is the failure here where you brake right away, after shifting to neutral.
Head-on vehicles and stalls on railroad tracks each have a rule that runs against instinct.

scenario.text: Jay is stalled on a railroad crossing when he sees a train coming from his left.

reasoning.text: The guide says unbuckle, get out and away from the tracks, running toward the direction the train is coming from to avoid flying debris.

result.text: Jay gets out and moves away from the tracks toward his left, the side the train is coming from.

claim.text: Common mistake: running away from the train in the direction it is heading.

correction.text: Running in the direction the train is heading puts you in the path of debris; run toward the direction it is coming from.

memory_support.text: Stuck pedal: neutral, brake. Train coming: run toward where it comes from.

prompt.text: Jay's accelerator sticks in traffic. What should he do with the gear selector and the brake, and when may he turn off the key?

answer.text: Shift to neutral and brake, then turn off the ignition only after stopping and no longer needing to steer.

rationale.text: Turning off the key locks the steering in many vehicles, so the ignition waits until he has stopped.

lines.text: Stuck accelerator: neutral and brake.
Head-on: slow, pull right, horn.
Train coming: get out and away.

narration.text: This last lesson of the chapter covers a stuck accelerator, a vehicle coming at you head-on, a stall on railroad tracks, and a safety finding about large passenger vans. A stuck accelerator is unusual because it calls for braking right away, after shifting to neutral, while the ignition waits until you have stopped. A vehicle coming at you head-on in your lane calls for slowing down, pulling to the right and sounding your horn, not swerving into the left lane. On the tracks, what you do depends on whether a train is coming. And the NTSB has a finding about twelve- and fifteen-passenger vans.

lines.text: Shift to neutral and brake.
Watch the road; horn and flashers warn others.
Steer off; look for a way out.

narration.text: For a stuck accelerator, the guide lists the steps. Shift to neutral, brake, keep watching the road, warn others with the horn and flashers, and steer safely off the road. While you slow down, keep looking for a way out of traffic. Then the ignition. With a stuck accelerator, turn off the ignition only after stopping and no longer needing to steer, since turning off the key locks the steering in many vehicles. This ties back to the general emergency rule that with power steering or a locking steering wheel you never turn off the ignition until fully stopped. Neutral and brakes come first, and the key comes last.

lines.text: Stuck accelerator: neutral and brake right away.
Blowout: avoid the brakes at first.
Name the failure, then the first step.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A stuck accelerator calls for shifting to neutral and braking right away, unlike a blowout, where you avoid the brakes at first. Both are sudden emergencies at speed, and questions like to mix up their first steps. In a blowout you grip the wheel firmly, lift off the accelerator without braking, and let the car slow until it is nearly stopped and off the road before braking. With a stuck accelerator, the brakes come in right away, after the shift to neutral. And with brake failure, a third case, you pump the pedal fast and hard. Name the failure first, then pick its first step.

lines.text: Slow down and pull to the right.
Sound your horn.
Do not swerve into the left lane.

narration.text: If a vehicle comes at you head-on in your lane, slow down, pull to the right and sound your horn, but do not swerve into the left lane. The guide explains why the left lane is a bad escape. Swerving into the left lane to avoid a head-on vehicle is dangerous because the other driver may move back into that same lane. So the right side is your direction. Slowing down, pulling to the right and using the horn are the actions the guide gives, and swerving into the left lane stays off the list. Remember the reason with the rule: the other driver may move back into that very lane you swerved into.

lines.text: Unbuckle and get out.
Get away from the tracks.
Run toward where the train comes from.

narration.text: If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks with a train coming, unbuckle, get out and away from the tracks, running toward the direction the train is coming from, to avoid flying debris. That direction can feel backward, so learn the reason with it. Running in the direction the train is heading after a stall puts you in the path of debris when the train strikes your vehicle. By moving away from the tracks and toward the side the train is coming from, you stay out of that path. So there are two parts: get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, and choose the direction the train is coming from, not the one it is heading.

lines.text: Roll down the windows to listen.
Try to restart the vehicle.
If that fails, neutral and push it off.

narration.text: The other railroad case is a stall with no train in sight. If you stall on the tracks with no train in sight, roll down the windows to listen, and try to restart. If that fails, shift to neutral and push the vehicle off the tracks. The open windows let you listen for a train while you work. Keep the two cases apart. With a train coming, you unbuckle, get out and get away, running toward the direction the train is coming from. With no train in sight, you listen, try to restart, and push the vehicle off in neutral if it will not start. The deciding question is whether a train is coming.

lines.text: Jay's accelerator sticks in traffic.
Gear and brake: what does he do?
When can the key go off?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Jay is driving in traffic when his accelerator sticks. What should he do with the gear selector and the brake, and when may he turn off the ignition? Work it out before reading on. He should shift to neutral and brake, keep watching the road, warn others with the horn and flashers, and steer safely off the road while looking for a way out of traffic. He turns off the ignition only after stopping and no longer needing to steer, since turning off the key locks the steering in many vehicles. Unlike a blowout, where you avoid the brakes at first, a stuck accelerator calls for braking right away.

lines.text: Twelve- and fifteen-passenger vans.
Unstable with more than ten passengers.
NTSB recommends special driver training.

narration.text: To close the chapter, a finding about large passenger vans. The NTSB has found that twelve- and fifteen-passenger vans are inherently unstable when loaded as designed with more than ten passengers, and it recommends special training for their drivers. The NTSB points drivers of large passenger vans to its website for more on van safety. Then recall this lesson's emergencies. A stuck accelerator: neutral, brake, warn others, steer off, and the key off only after stopping. A head-on vehicle: slow, pull right, sound the horn, no swerve left. A stall with a train coming: get out and run toward the direction the train is coming from.
